strengths: As an extension of Data2Vec, I-JEPA etc class of work to videos, it is a useful baseline for the community to know.
The experiments and methodology are clear and easy to understand.
The paper is a nicely executed empirical study that extends I-JEPA [Assran et al, 2023) to video data
(pre)training on video data can be fast by decoding/predicting in latent space, and the paper shows empirically that there may not be a need to sacrifice performance for speed.

Empirical evaluations with "frozen" backbones (encoders) are conducted with academic video and standard image benchmarks that suggest that representations on video work better on video data while being competitive on image benchmarks.
The paper idea is quite simple and straight forward. It shares the same high-level idea as the MAE.
While the MAE focuses on predicting the patch, the proposed idea focuses on predicting the embedding of the patch.
The proposed approach achieves quite significant performance boost on all the datasets, which is a little bit surprising.
If the proposed approach and its performance can be verified, then it might be a quite good paper for the community to have.
The fundamental training method is crtical for both image and video representation learning.
The method seems to be sound.
The biggest strength of this work is the large-scale training on a huge dataset (VideoMix2M), showing the ability of JEPA to scale up.
This work is evaluated on six different tasks/datasets (3 for videos and 3 for images), which provides a solid baseline for future methods.
weaknesses: As a extension of I-JEPA to videos, technical novelty is extremely limited.
Evaluations are problematic, by either not comparing to the relevant work or by comparing to prior work in a misleading way, contrary to the evaluation protocols the whole community has been using.

Most recent related work has adopted a finetuning evaluation protocol (e.g. VideoMAE, VideoMAEv2, ST-MAE, Hiera, MaskFeat, OmniMAE, MCMAE) and yet such evaluation is almost entirely absent from this work, portraying a highly misleading picture of the state of the literature and the capabilities of the V-JEPA models.
Notably missing are references/discussion and comparison to some of the stronger recent work (e.g. UnMasked Teacher, Li et al 2023; Hiera, Ryali et al 2023; MCMAE, Gao et al, 2022, etc).
Transfer to images is also explored, but comparison to prior work is problematic, notably missing any comparison to VITO, Parthasarathy et al, 2023.

The sample efficiency discussion is problematic in several ways, e.g. numbers of images are being compared to number of videos (Table 12), and the claim that a shorter training schedule in epochs is more efficient is not meaningful; wall‑clock training time would be a more appropriate metric.
Speedup reported in Table 11 may be an artifact of larger training data and model size rather than methodological improvement.

The method proposed in the paper is an extension of I-JEPA to video. The masking across the temporal dimension ("3D‑multiblock") and latent space prediction borrow heavily from I-JEPA, limiting novelty.
A key component that determines the success of VJPEA is the multiblock design; the paper lacks careful ablation of design choices such as scale factors and aspect ratios used to design the mask.
The evaluation scheme (attentive probing) may make it hard for readers to compare performance across publications.
The paper writing should be improved; the methodology part is quite hard to read, especially the application to video (sect. 3.2).
It is unclear how to obtain the 3D sin‑cos positional embedding mentioned in the Predictor section after the input has been processed by the 3D ConvNet into a 1D feature.
It is unclear how to obtain the self‑supervised video features: whether they are the output of the target encoder or the context encoder.
For a fair comparison with VideoMAE, the proposed approach should be pretrained on the Kinetics400 dataset.

Such self‑distillation style has been widely used in the literature (mean teacher); the teacher‑student framework for representation learning is not novel, and applying it to masked regions does not fundamentally alter the approach.

Mask modeling and predicting latent features of masked spatio‑temporal regions has been investigated in prior work (e.g., UMT); the paper does not sufficiently differentiate its approach from existing methods.
Results in the abstract and Figure 1 are difficult to assess because model sizes differ, making it unclear whether gains are due to the method or a larger model.
The pretraining data (VideoMix2M) differs from others, raising doubt about whether improvements stem from the self‑supervised method or the dataset.
Finetuning results on standard video benchmarks (e.g., K400, SthV2) for SOTA comparison are missing.
Using an existing image architecture to process videos by flattening 3D feature maps into 1D does not qualify as an architectural novelty.
The paper does not address video‑specific challenges such as covering larger temporal context (>2 seconds) or capturing long‑term dependencies (e.g., H‑JEPA?).
The experimental protocol is flawed; tables do not show results when the model is trained on the same datasets as competing methods, making fair comparison impossible.
Figure 1 (Left) compares models of different sizes, preventing direct comparison.

Ablation results indicate that when trained on the same K400 data, VideoMAE outperforms the proposed method on SSv2 (61.2 vs 50.8) and on ImageNet‑1k (71.9 vs 66.1), so V‑JEPA is not SOTA under equal conditions.
The paper provides ablations on masking strategy but lacks ablations on stride and temporal receptive field, which are important for video models.
Additional ablations on longer clips (>2 seconds) or two‑flow architectures (e.g., I3D with optical flow) would be more relevant for a video paper.
